newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN rights team details massacres by Kabila's forces.
newsitem.headline: UN rights team details massacres by Kabila's forces.

text.p: The U.N. investigator banned by the new Congo government has pointed to 134 separate massacres of Rwandan refugees by forces allied to Laurent Kabila before he became president.

Roberto Garreton of Chile, in a July 2 report released by the United Nations on Friday, said evidence appeared to point to genocide and systematic executions. He suggested the perpetrators go before an international war crimes tribunal.
He also said that killings and other grave human rights violations had not stopped after Kabila became president of the Democratic Repubic of the Congo.

His new U.N. Human Rights Commission report did not estimate how many people were killed but said eyewitnesses and U.N. relief workers gave evidence of more than 180 incidents of massacres in the former Zaire.

Of that number, Garreton said 134 were traced to rebels loyal to Kabila and his Tutsi allies. The remainder were committed by the former Zairean army under ousted President Mobuto Sese Seko or Rwandan Hutu militia that controlled the refugee camps.

The methods used were "deliberate, premeditated massacres, the dispersal of refugees to inaccessible inhospitable areas, the systematic blockade of humanitarian assistance and the stubborn opposition thus far to any attempt to conduct an impartial objective investigation into the very serious allegations," the report said.

Over a million Hutus in 1994 crossed into what was then Zaire fearing reprisals for the genocide in Rwanda of minority Tutsis by Hutu hardliners. The bulk returned home, but U.N. relief officials say up to 200,000 remain unaccounted for.

Hutu militants had used the camps as havens to rebuild their strength and conduct guerrilla raids against the Rwanda government, controlled by Tutsis who were instrumental in the rebellion against Mobutu.
"One cannot, of course ignore the presence of persons guilty of genocide, soldiers and milita members among the refugees," the report said.

"It is nevertheless unacceptable to claim that more than 1 million people, including large numbers of children, should be collectively designated as persons guilty of genocide and liable to execution without trial," it said.
Garreton, a respected human rights lawyer, has been denied further entry to the country by Kabila's government after his earlier report that cited 40 massacre sites.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan this week said he would organise the investigation himself, without Garreton, so it could be undertaken quickly. Both Annan and the United States have been criticised by human rights groups for not having put pressure on Kabila to allow Garreton to continue.

The new, harsher report, was based on interviews with survivors in Rwanda and other eyewitnesses of the attacks against refugee camps in Uvira, Bukavu, Goma and especially Kivu in eastern Zaire since last October.
Garreton expressed concern at continuing allegations of killings and other violations, particularly in the Kivu area.

"In this connection, the summary executions, which accompanied the seizure of power in Kinshasa, bear out concerns about the action of (Kabila's) soldiers out of the range of the cameras and raise worrying questions about their future role in a society that is supposedly making the transition to democracy," his report said..
